title: Trade talks between top Canada, U.S. officials ramping up: sources
summary: As talks with the Trump administration begin to ramp up once again, the prime minister's point man on Canada-U.S. trade has been meeting with his counterparts weekly in a more formal way, according…

image.caption: Chief trade negotiator Janice Charette and Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc arrive at a committee meeting in Ottawa on Tuesday. Sources tell CBC News that trade talks with the Trump administration are again ramping up. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

As talks with the Trump administration begin to ramp up once again, the prime minister's point man on Canada-U.S. trade has been meeting with his counterparts weekly in a more formal way, according to three senior government officials.
No formal deal is on the table, work underway to reduce trade irritants

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has not travelled to Washington, D.C., to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer or Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick since talks restarted earlier this month. But there have been phone and video calls happening on a regular basis, the sources say.
Canada's chief trade negotiator Janice Charette is usually also on these calls, according to the officials.
CBC News is not naming the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the trade talks.
Canada urged to ramp up U.S outreach as Democrats target Trump's tariffs

The sources say while there is no formal deal on the table, both sides are working to remove trade irritants with the goal of eventually getting to one. Auto and steel tariffs remain key sticking points.

At this time, there are no plans for LeBlanc to travel to Washington for in-person talks, unlike over the summer, where both LeBlanc and Charette spent weeks working from the Canadian Embassy and met regularly at the U.S. trade representative's office.
But no deal was reached, and when talks fell apart the U.S. hit Canada with additional tariffs, prompting Canada to respond with countermeasures.
On Nov. 1, Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on social media saying teams from both countries would start working again on a trade deal.

"We all recognize that this period of trade uncertainty has created real challenges for Canadian businesses, workers, communities and of course the families of those affected," said LeBlanc at the international trade committee on Tuesday.

"We believe it is possible to make a deal that is, first and foremost, in the interest of Canada, but also in the interest of the United States, and ultimately also with our Mexican partners," he said in French.

blocks.text: The Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations — a group of experts appointed by the federal government — are set to meet virtually on Thursday, where they are expected to discuss the situation on the ground in Washington and how financial support for tariff-affected industries is being implemented.
It will be the first meeting since the midterm elections, which saw the Trump administration lose control of Congress.
Democratic lawmakers have pledged to repeal tariffs on Canadian goods, although Democrats lack the two-thirds majorities in both chambers required to shield legislation from a presidential veto.
LeBlanc has said Canada's approach to finding a deal will not change despite the new political makeup of the U.S. Congress.
Goal is lowest tariffs possible: Charette
On Tuesday, Charette was asked by Conservative Canada-U.S. trade critic Shuvaloy Majumdar about whether Canada is now looking for a deal without tariffs.

"Madame Charette, you had suggested long-term tariffs are something we might have to accept. Would you say that tariff-free trade is now off the table, that's a decision the government has taken? Is the government's goal still tariff-free trade?"

blocks.text: Charette said the objective is to try to get as close as possible to tariff-free trade.
"I have suggested that we are trying to get to the lowest rate of tariffs on the narrowest basket of goods, with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers," she said.
"But we do have another partner on the other side of the table and they have shown to date an unwillingness to enter into any arrangement in which there is full tariff-free trade."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards.
